results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which describes the mushroom body as divided into these three parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle; and the mushroom body lobe system, consisting of a vertical branch and a medial branch with varying structures at different life stages. VFB holds various records related to the mushroom body, including images, neurons with parts in the mushroom body, and parts of the mushroom body itself, with specific counts available, such as [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body and [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body") parts of the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response:
The types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain include gamma Kenyon cells, as well as other types such as alpha/beta and alpha'/beta' Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes. VFB records show that there are several types of Kenyon cells, including KCab-c(i), KCab-c, KCg-m, Kenyon cell of main calyx, and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). The connectome data indicates that there are three main subtypes that project their axons to the gamma lobe, the alpha and beta lobes, and the alpha' and beta' lobes. 

VFB holds various data related to gamma Kenyon cell, including a list of available images, splits targeting gamma Kenyon cell, subclasses of gamma Kenyon cell, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, downstream connectivity classes, and upstream connectivity classes. To learn more about the specific types of Kenyon cells and their characteristics, you can run queries to retrieve the available data, such as the count of images of gamma Kenyon cell or the count of subclasses of gamma Kenyon cell.

results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response:
The adult Drosophila central brain contains approximately more than 125,000 neurons, according to the information from vfb, as retrieved by the VFB query. Note that this is a direct report from the query and not a count of neuron types annotated in VFB. For neuron types annotated in VFB, VFB does not currently hold specific data on the number of neuron types in the adult Drosophila central brain.

**Published neuron-count estimates — adult central brain** (from the literature):

- more than 125,000 neurons (adult Drosophila central brain connectome/model) — A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing. — PMID 39358519
- ~139,255 neurons (whole adult Drosophila brain) — Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain. — PMID 39358518

To determine the consistency of connectivity between the two datasets, you can run queries in VFB to compare the neurons connected to Fdg#1 (FAFB:16783943) and the neurons with some part in the ellipsoid body in the [EB on JRC_FlyEM_Hemibrain](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00101400 "Open EB on JRC_FlyEM_Hemibrain in Virtual Fly Brain") dataset. VFB has annotated data on neurons with similar morphology to Fdg#1 (FAFB:16783943) and neurons connected to it, as well as various aspects of the ellipsoid body, including neurons with some part in it, neurons with synaptic terminals in it, and images of neurons with some part in it. 

You can use the available VFB data to explore the connectivity of Fdg#1 (FAFB:16783943) and compare it with the connectivity data from the Hemibrain and FAFB datasets. However, VFB does not currently hold direct comparative data on the consistency of olfactory projection neuron connectivity between these two datasets.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior. According to VFB, it has a unique anatomy and connectivity. There is one giant fiber neuron per hemisphere, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum. It can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective. This axon enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle and descends on the ipsilateral side, in the dorsal cervical fasciculus. 

In the brain, the giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons. It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget. The giant fiber neuron enters the ventral nerve cord near the dorsal midline and extends posteroventrally to the mesothoracic neuromere, where it turns ventrolaterally and ends abruptly without branching. In the mesothoracic neuromere, it forms electrical synapses with downstream motor and premotor neurons at the inframedial bridge, where the two giant fiber neurons connect across the midline, and at the axonal lateral bend.

VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron is a primary neuron. Available driver lines for the giant fiber neuron include P{R48A11-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R30C01-p65.AD}, P{R68A06-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R25C08-p65.AD}, P{R79H02-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R14A01-p65.AD}, P{R79H02-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R25C08-p65.AD}, and P{VT004455-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R10A12-p65.AD}. 

Relevant publications for the giant fiber neuron include Phelan et al., 1996, King and Wyman, 1980, Stürner et al., 2025, Dorkenwald et al., 2024, Namiki et al., 2018, Thomas and Wyman, 1984, Koto et al., 1981, Power, 1948, Ito et al., 2014, Kamikouchi et al., 2009, Kennedy and Broadie, 2018, Allen et al., 1998, Bacon and Strausfeld, 1986, Matsuo et al., 2016, and Kim et al., 2020.

VFB has annotated [23](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of the giant fiber neuron, [5](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,SplitsTargeting "Run in VFB: Splits targeting DNp01") splits targeting it, and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") transgene expressions in it. The downstream connectivity classes for the giant fiber neuron include [389](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records, and the upstream connectivity classes include [472](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records.

results.title: Concepts: NBLAST
results.question: What is NBLAST and what does an NBLAST similarity score mean?
results.response: NBLAST is a method to quantify morphological similarity. According to the documentation, its similarity score is calculated by finding the closest tangent vector in the target neuron for each tangent vector in the query neuron, and then calculating a score from the distance between and the dot product of the two vectors, with the final score typically normalized to a self-self comparison, where a perfect match would be 1. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain documentation, which cites Costa et al., 2016. VFB does not currently hold additional data on the interpretation of NBLAST similarity scores beyond this documentation.
